cards.front: Why can a membrane phospholipid or protein not easily flip to the other leaflet of a bilayer on its own?
cards.back: Its polar head group, or polar stretch of protein, crosses the bilayer's oily core only rarely.
cards.quote: a polar head group, or a polar stretch of protein, crosses it only rarely.

cards.front: The face of a membrane that touches the outside of the cell or an organelle lumen is the {{c1::exoplasmic face}} (or noncytosolic face): the one that never touches cytosol.
cards.quote: That second face is the exoplasmic face (or noncytosolic face): the one that never touches cytosol.

cards.front: Which membrane lipids flip between leaflets quickly on their own, and what lets them?
cards.back: Cholesterol, ceramide and diacylglycerol. Their small uncharged head groups cross the oily core easily, so the slow-flip rule applies to phospholipids with polar head groups.
cards.quote: Cholesterol, ceramide and diacylglycerol, with small uncharged head groups, flip quickly on their own

cards.front: After a protein is inserted at the ER, why does membrane traffic on the secretory and endocytic routes never carry it across a bilayer?
cards.back: Membrane then moves only by budding and fusion, and neither process carries anything across a bilayer.
cards.quote: After that, membrane traffic carries it between compartments, and budding and fusion move nothing across a bilayer.

cards.front: Which compartment lumens sit on the same topological side as the outside of the cell?
cards.back: The lumens of the ER (including the nuclear envelope space), Golgi, secretory vesicles, endosomes and lysosomes.
cards.quote: So the lumens of the ER, Golgi, secretory vesicles, endosomes and lysosomes all sit on the same side as the outside of the cell.
cards.section: The rule: a lumen counts as outside

cards.front: What does it mean that the endosome lumen is "topologically equivalent" to the outside of the cell?
cards.back: You can get from one space to the other by budding and fusion alone, never passing through a membrane. The endosome lumen was the outside.
cards.quote: you can get from one space to the other by budding and fusing alone, without ever passing through a membrane.
cards.section: The rule: a lumen counts as outside

cards.front: A patch of plasma membrane dimples inward and pinches off as an endocytic vesicle. What fills the vesicle, and which face of its membrane touches the cytosol?
cards.back: Extracellular fluid fills it. The face that touched the cytosol still does; the face that met the outside now faces the lumen.
cards.why: Nothing crossed the membrane. It only changed shape.
cards.quote: A gulp of extracellular fluid: the sac closed around fluid that was outside the cell a moment earlier.
cards.section: The rule: a lumen counts as outside

cards.front: When a transport vesicle fuses with its target membrane, which leaflets merge and which spaces join?
cards.back: The two cytosol-facing leaflets merge, and the two lumens (or a lumen and the outside of the cell) join. So fusion never swaps faces.
cards.quote: when a vesicle fuses with its target, the two cytosol-facing leaflets merge, and the two lumens (or a lumen and the outside) join.
cards.section: The rule: a lumen counts as outside

cards.front: For a protein of the secretory pathway, when and through what is its membrane orientation normally set?
cards.back: When it enters the ER membrane, usually through the translocon, the channel that threads new chains into or across the membrane.
cards.quote: it is normally set when the protein enters the ER membrane, usually through the translocon
cards.section: The rule: a lumen counts as outside

cards.front: Why are N-linked glycans added only to parts of a protein that sit in the ER lumen?
cards.back: The enzyme that adds them, oligosaccharyl transferase, has its active site on the lumenal side of the ER membrane.
cards.quote: the enzyme that adds it, oligosaccharyl transferase, has its active site on the lumenal side.
cards.section: The rule: a lumen counts as outside

cards.front: A type I single-pass protein carries an N-linked glycan on its N-terminal domain. It travels ER → Golgi → plasma membrane, then is taken back in by endocytosis. Where is the glycan at the plasma membrane and in the endosome, and where is the C terminus throughout?
cards.back: Glycan: extracellular at the plasma membrane, in the endosome lumen after endocytosis. The C terminus stays in the cytosol at every step.
cards.why: The glycan's part of the chain crossed once, in the ER, and budding and fusion never flip it.
cards.quote: The sugar and N terminus face the endosome lumen; the C terminus faces the cytosol.
cards.section: The rule: a lumen counts as outside

cards.front: Influenza spike proteins are made in the ER with their sugar-carrying ends in the lumen. The virus then buds outward from the plasma membrane. Where do the sugar-carrying ends sit on the finished virus?
cards.back: On the outside of the virus.
cards.why: The ER lumen is topologically outside; at the plasma membrane those ends face out, and outward budding keeps them on the virus surface.
cards.quote: its spike proteins, made in the ER with their sugar-carrying ends in the lumen, stud the outside of the virus.
cards.section: The rule: a lumen counts as outside

cards.front: A membrane protein's {{c1::topology}} is which of its parts face the cytosol and which face the other side.
cards.quote: A membrane protein's topology is which of its parts face the cytosol and which face the other side.

cards.front: Single-pass membrane proteins: where are the N and C termini of a type I protein, and of a type II protein?
cards.back: Type I: N terminus in the lumen or outside, C terminus in the cytosol. Type II: N terminus in the cytosol, C terminus in the lumen or outside.
cards.why: Examples: glycophorin A and the EGF receptor are type I; the transferrin receptor and many Golgi glycosyltransferases are type II.
cards.quote: Single-pass type II: one segment, N terminus in the cytosol, C terminus in the lumen or outside.

cards.front: What defines a multipass membrane protein, and what is one example?
cards.back: Several membrane-spanning segments, with loops alternating between the two faces. The glucose transporter GLUT1 is one.
cards.quote: Multipass: several segments, with loops alternating between the two faces.

cards.front: A GPI-anchored protein has no membrane-spanning segment. Why does it end up on the lumenal leaflet, and so on the outer face of the plasma membrane?
cards.back: The glycosylphosphatidylinositol anchor is attached in the ER lumen, so the protein sits on the lumenal leaflet, which becomes the outer leaflet after traffic.
cards.why: Prion protein and alkaline phosphatase are held this way.
cards.quote: the protein is attached by a glycolipid, glycosylphosphatidylinositol (GPI), to the lumenal leaflet, because the anchor is attached in the ER lumen.

cards.front: Many Golgi glycosyltransferases, the enzymes that build sugar chains, are type II single-pass proteins. Which terminus sits in the Golgi lumen, and which in the cytosol?
cards.back: The C terminus is in the Golgi lumen; the N terminus is in the cytosol.
cards.why: Type II puts the C terminus in the ER lumen, and every lumen on the secretory route counts as the same side.
cards.quote: Type II puts the C terminus in the ER lumen, and every lumen on the route counts as outside.

cards.front: Can vesicle traffic flip the orientation of a finished membrane protein?
cards.back: No. Reorientation normally happens during insertion; a few proteins rearrange later while still in the ER membrane, but traffic never flips a finished protein.
cards.why: Aquaporin-1 is the textbook case of a protein that changes topology after insertion in the ER.
cards.quote: Reorientation normally happens during insertion, though a few proteins rearrange later in the ER membrane; a finished protein is not flipped by traffic.

cards.front: In a protease protection test of membrane protein topology, what are microsomes and why are they used?
cards.back: Sealed vesicles of ER membrane made by breaking cells, with the lumen still inside. A protease added outside cannot reach what is lumenal.
cards.quote: The standard test uses microsomes: sealed vesicles of ER membrane, made by breaking cells, with the lumen still inside.
cards.section: How we know which way a protein faces

cards.front: In a protease protection test on sealed microsomes, why add detergent before the protease in a control sample?
cards.back: Detergent opens the membrane. If the surviving tag is now digested, its survival was protection by the membrane, not a protease-proof tag.
cards.quote: The detergent control shows that tag could be digested once the membrane was opened, so its survival was protection, not a protease-proof tag.
cards.section: How we know which way a protein faces

cards.front: A single-pass protein is tagged at both ends and made in sealed microsomes. After protease, the C-terminal tag is still detected and the N-terminal tag is gone; with detergent first, both are gone. What is the orientation?
cards.back: C terminus in the lumen, N terminus in the cytosol: type II.
cards.why: Protease cannot enter a sealed vesicle, so the surviving tag was lumenal; the detergent control rules out a protease-proof tag.
cards.quote: Tag the protein's two ends with different epitopes, short tags an antibody recognizes, and add a protease.
cards.section: How we know which way a protein faces

cards.front: Sealed ER microsomes carrying a GPI-anchored protein are treated with protease, with no detergent. Is the protein digested?
cards.back: No. It is protected.
cards.why: The GPI anchor is attached in the ER lumen, so the protein sits on the lumenal leaflet, and a protease cannot enter a sealed vesicle.
cards.quote: A protease cannot enter a sealed vesicle, so the tag that survived was in the lumen.
cards.section: How we know which way a protein faces

cards.front: An N-X-S/T glycosylation site is placed in the C-terminal domain of a new single-pass protein, and the protein made in the ER shows a sugar gel shift. What does that show?
cards.back: The C-terminal end reached the ER lumen.
cards.why: A site becomes glycosylated only in the lumen. The reverse does not hold: an unused site does not by itself prove that end stayed in the cytosol.
cards.quote: A site becomes glycosylated only in the lumen.

cards.front: In cultured cells, an epitope on an ER membrane protein is detected after Triton X-100 but not after low digitonin. Where does the epitope face?
cards.back: The ER lumen.
cards.why: Low digitonin opens the cholesterol-rich plasma membrane but leaves ER and Golgi membranes largely closed; Triton X-100 opens all membranes.
cards.quote: Low digitonin permeabilizes the cholesterol-rich plasma membrane but leaves ER and Golgi membranes largely closed; Triton X-100 opens all membranes.

cards.front: How does alkaline extraction tell an integrated membrane protein from a peripheral one?
cards.back: High pH strips peripheral proteins; an integrated protein stays in the membrane pellet.
cards.quote: High pH strips peripheral proteins; an integrated protein stays in the membrane pellet.

cards.front: Intact cells displaying the type II transferrin receptor at the plasma membrane are exposed to a protease or antibody that cannot enter cells. Which end of the receptor is reachable?
cards.back: The C-terminal end, which faces outside. The N terminus, in the cytosol, is not reachable.
cards.why: Type II puts the C terminus in the ER lumen, which becomes the outside at the plasma membrane; this extends the sealed-microsome protease-protection logic.
cards.quote: The C terminus both times. Type II puts the C terminus in the ER lumen, and every lumen on the route counts as outside.

cards.front: In the human red blood cell membrane, which phospholipids sit mainly in the outer leaflet?
cards.back: Phosphatidylcholine (PC) and sphingomyelin. PS and PE sit mainly on the inner, cytoplasmic leaflet.
cards.quote: phosphatidylcholine (PC) and sphingomyelin mainly on the outer leaflet
cards.section: Lipids: the side the cell has to keep pumping

cards.front: Spontaneous phospholipid flip-flop takes hours or longer. Why does a red blood cell still need constant pumping to keep its lipid asymmetry?
cards.back: Slow is not zero. Over the months a red blood cell lives, leakage alone would wear away any pattern set up at the start.
cards.quote: Slow is not zero: over the months a red blood cell lives, leakage alone would wear away any pattern set up at the start.
cards.section: Lipids: the side the cell has to keep pumping

cards.front: Flippase, floppase, scramblase: which way does each move lipid, and which use ATP?
cards.back: Flippase: outer to cytoplasmic leaflet, uses ATP. Floppase: cytoplasmic to outer leaflet, uses ATP. Scramblase: both ways, down the gradients, generally no ATP.
cards.why: Flip is in, flop is out, scramble is both ways. Flippases chiefly move PS and PE; most are P4-type ATPases.
cards.quote: flip is in, flop is out, scramble is both ways.
cards.section: Lipids: the side the cell has to keep pumping

cards.front: Why is plasma-membrane lipid asymmetry described as a steady state rather than a frozen pattern?
cards.back: Pumps push lipids one way while slow leakage and regulated scramblases push the other. Switching on a scramblase collapses it far faster than spontaneous flip-flop.
cards.quote: So plasma-membrane asymmetry is a steady state: pumps push one way, slow leakage and regulated scramblases push the other
cards.section: Lipids: the side the cell has to keep pumping

cards.front: What does the calcium-activated scramblase TMEM16F do in activated platelets, and why does it matter?
cards.back: It can expose phosphatidylserine on the platelet surface, where the negatively charged lipid supports blood clotting.
cards.quote: Its activity can expose PS on the surface of activated platelets, where the negatively charged lipid supports blood clotting.
cards.section: Lipids: the side the cell has to keep pumping

cards.front: A red blood cell runs out of ATP, with calcium unchanged. How fast does phosphatidylserine appear on its outer surface, and why?
cards.back: Slowly, over hours or longer.
cards.why: Flippases stop, but PS can only leak outward by spontaneous flip-flop. A calcium-opened scramblase would carry it across within minutes.
cards.quote: With no ATP the flippases stop, but PS can still only leak outward by spontaneous flip-flop, so it creeps out over hours or longer.
cards.section: Lipids: the side the cell has to keep pumping

cards.front: Platelets are activated with a calcium rise while a drug blocks TMEM16F, the calcium-activated scramblase. Predict the effect on surface phosphatidylserine and on the platelets' support of clotting.
cards.back: If TMEM16F is the route, less PS would be expected at the surface, so the platelets would likely give less support to blood clotting.
cards.why: Rests on two stated points: TMEM16F activity can expose PS on activated platelets, and surface PS, a negatively charged lipid, supports clotting.
cards.quote: TMEM16F is the best-studied calcium-activated scramblase.
cards.section: Lipids: the side the cell has to keep pumping

cards.front: The fluid mosaic model predicts what about a membrane protein's orientation and its movement?
cards.back: Each protein keeps a fixed orientation across the membrane but moves freely within its plane.
cards.quote: proteins keep a fixed orientation across the membrane but are free to move within its plane.

cards.front: In fluorescence recovery after photobleaching (FRAP), why does the bleached spot brighten again?
cards.back: Unbleached molecules diffuse in. The bleached molecules are still there and still moving; they are simply dark.
cards.quote: If they are mobile, unbleached ones diffuse in and the spot brightens.

cards.front: FRAP on a membrane protein, corrected intensities: before the bleach Fi = 100, immediately after F0 = 25, plateau F∞ = 70. What are the mobile and immobile fractions?
cards.back: Mobile fraction = (F∞ − F0) / (Fi − F0) = (70 − 25) / (100 − 25) = 45 / 75 = 0.60. Immobile fraction = 0.40.
cards.why: The denominator is the bleached amount, 75, not 100: only what was bleached can recover.
cards.quote: The denominator is 80, not 100: only what was bleached can recover.

cards.front: FRAP data: Fi = 100, F0 = 25, plateau F∞ = 70. The recovery curve reads 47.5 at 3.0 s and 50 at 3.4 s. What is the recovery half-time?
cards.back: Half the recoverable increment is (70 − 25) / 2 = 22.5, so half recovery is at 25 + 22.5 = 47.5. t½ = 3.0 s.
cards.why: Halve the recovered increase, not the prebleach value; 50 would give the wrong time.
cards.quote: Always halve the recovered increase, not the prebleach value.

cards.front: A FRAP plateau reaches 80 after bleaching from 100 to 20, so a quarter of the bleached signal never recovers. Does this show that a quarter of the protein is anchored to the cytoskeleton?
cards.back: No. The immobile fraction does not say why the signal stayed dark.
cards.why: Anchoring to the cytoskeleton, bleaching a large share of the cell's total pool, or bleaching during imaging can each lower the plateau.
cards.quote: Anchoring to the cytoskeleton, bleaching a large share of the cell's total pool, or bleaching during imaging can each lower the plateau.

cards.front: A circular spot of radius w = 1.5 µm on a flat plasma membrane is bleached instantly and uniformly, and recovery by two-dimensional diffusion has t½ = 2.0 s. Using D ≈ 0.224 w²/t½, estimate D.
cards.why: Valid only under the model: instantaneous uniform bleach, flat membrane, large unbleached reservoir, recovery by diffusion alone.
cards.quote: Assume the bleach is instantaneous and uniform, the membrane is flat, the unbleached reservoir is large, and recovery is by two-dimensional diffusion alone.

cards.front: In diffusion-limited FRAP, why does the recovery half-time depend on the square of the spot radius rather than the radius?
cards.back: Diffusion time grows with distance squared, so t½ is proportional to w² / D.
cards.quote: Diffusion time grows with distance squared, not distance, so t½ is proportional to w² / D.

cards.front: FRAP is repeated on the same cells with the bleach radius doubled, and the half-time stays near its original value. What would this point to, and should D be computed from 0.224 w²/t½?
cards.back: It points to recovery limited by binding and release rather than diffusion, so the diffusion formula should not be used.
cards.why: Pure diffusion would make t½ grow four times when w doubles; binding-limited recovery breaks the w² scaling.
cards.quote: If the half-time had stayed near 4.0 s, that would point to recovery limited by binding and release rather than diffusion

cards.front: About how does lateral diffusion of a membrane-bound molecule compare with a protein free in the cytoplasm?
cards.back: More than a hundred times slower: in a table by Day and colleagues, cholera toxin B bound to the plasma membrane of COS-7 and MEF cells at 37 °C diffuses at about 0.2 µm²/s, versus about 40 µm²/s for free EGFP in COS-7 cytoplasm.
cards.quote: more than a hundred times slower than a protein free in the cytoplasm

cards.front: Name two things that limit the sideways movement of molecules in a plasma membrane.
cards.back: Tight junctions separate apical from basolateral membrane in epithelia, and an actin meshwork under the membrane can slow some molecules.
cards.quote: Tight junctions separate apical from basolateral membrane in epithelia, and an actin meshwork under the membrane can slow some molecules.

cards.front: What are lipid rafts proposed to be, and how settled is their existence in living cells?
cards.back: Proposed ordered domains rich in cholesterol and sphingolipid. Their existence, size and composition in living cells are unresolved.
cards.why: A detergent-resistant membrane fraction is not a native raft; detergent can create or rearrange domains.
cards.quote: reviews describe their existence, size and composition in living cells as unresolved, not as one settled universal structure

cards.front: A nuclear protein carries an O-GlcNAc sugar. Does the sugar face a lumen or the outside of the cell?
cards.back: Neither. It stays in the nucleus, on the cytosol side.
cards.why: Where a sugar is added decides where it ends up. O-GlcNAc is added in the cytosol and nucleus, so "glycans always face outside" is wrong.
cards.quote: O-GlcNAc added in the cytosol and nucleus stays there.

cards.front: Misfolded proteins in the ER lumen are destroyed in the cytosol. Does this break the rule that membrane traffic never moves anything across a bilayer?
cards.back: No. ER-associated degradation (ERAD) is a dedicated machine that pulls them back to the cytosol.
cards.why: The rule's first clause: crossing a bilayer at a useful speed takes a dedicated machine. Budding and fusion still never carry anything across.
cards.quote: ER-associated degradation (ERAD) pulls misfolded proteins back to the cytosol to be destroyed.

cards.front: Can the lumen-counts-as-outside rule predict how a mitochondrial membrane protein made in the cytosol faces its membranes?
cards.back: No. Mitochondria import most proteins from the cytosol across their own membranes and are not joined to the secretory pathway by vesicle routes.
cards.quote: Mitochondria and chloroplasts import most of their proteins from the cytosol across their own membranes and are not joined to the secretory pathway by the ordinary vesicle routes.

cards.front: An autophagosome wraps a pocket of cytosol. Which face of the membrane wrapped directly around that pocket faces the trapped cytosol?
cards.back: Its cytosolic face. Wrapping is not an exception to the topology rule.
cards.why: The membrane only changes shape around the pocket, as in endocytosis, so no face swaps sides.
cards.quote: the membrane wrapped directly around each pocket keeps its cytosolic face toward it.

cards.front: A type I plasma-membrane protein with an N-linked glycan on its N-terminal domain is endocytosed and later delivered to a lysosome by vesicle traffic. Where are the glycan and the C terminus?
cards.back: The glycan faces the lysosome lumen; the C terminus faces the cytosol.
cards.why: The lysosome lumen is on the outside side of the topology, and budding and fusion never swap faces.
cards.quote: So the face that met the cytosol always meets the cytosol
